articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
This amendment updates existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy towards the country.
Further details regarding the scope and specific provisions of the amended general license are available on the Treasury Department's website.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Related to North Korea and DRC
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
These actions aim to counter illicit activities and threats posed by these regions, aligning with U.S. foreign policy and national security objectives.
The specific reasons for these designations and the identities of the sanctioned parties are detailed in the official announcement.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement with OFAC
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026.
The settlement resolves potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs.
Further details of the settlement, including the nature of the violations and the penalty amount, are available in the official OFAC announcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
These updates provide additional guidance and clarification for financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations under U.S. sanctions programs.
The amended FAQs are intended to help improve understanding and adherence to OFAC regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, OFAC announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.
The agency also issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.
These actions reflect a dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting measures based on evolving geopolitical circumstances and policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026.
These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses to guide compliance.
The PAIPA designations aim to combat the theft of American intellectual property and protect national economic interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: On October 16, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question.
These updates aim to clarify and adjust the scope of authorized transactions involving Venezuela, reflecting ongoing U.S. policy considerations.
The changes are intended to provide further guidance to individuals and entities engaging in activities related to the country.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on these actions.
These measures are part of ongoing efforts to address threats posed by these regimes and ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.
This action signifies a targeted adjustment to the U.S. sanctions program concerning Venezuela.
The delisting reflects a reassessment of the circumstances surrounding the previously designated entity or individual.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These actions are part of a broader strategy to disrupt illicit networks that pose threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
The designations aim to sever financial ties and limit the operational capabilities of these illicit actors.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Designating 1,569 Individuals and Entities
body: The European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, adding 1,569 individuals and entities to its sanctions lists.

This package, described as one of the most significant sanctions developments since 2022, includes 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals, bringing the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.
The measures primarily focus on listings and asset freezes, targeting Russia's military-industrial complex and individuals involved in recent legislative elections held in disputed territories.

articles.headline: EU Adds Three Individuals and Four Entities to DPRK Sanctions List
body: On October 12, 2026, the Council of the European Union added three individuals and four entities to the EU's autonomous DPRK sanctions list.

These designations target those supporting or facilitating activities contributing to North Korea's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, and other weapons of mass destruction programs, or for violating and evading UN sanctions.
The measures specifically address activities connected with increasing DPRK-Russia military and economic cooperation.

articles.headline: EU Lists Individuals and Entities for Sanctions Circumvention
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures on October 15, 2026, against three individuals and nine entities.
These entities are involved in the import of sanctioned goods to Russia and in the circumvention of EU sanctions related to oil and financial transactions.
The listings were made under the EU's restrictive measures framework targeting actions undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence.

articles.headline: UK Expands Russia Sanctions with 38 New Designations
body: The United Kingdom expanded its Russia-related sanctions on October 8, 2026, through a package comprising 38 new designations.

This follows an earlier package on October 1, 2026, which targeted individuals involved in the detention and mistreatment of Ukrainian civilians, deportation of Ukrainian children, and pro-Kremlin disinformation activities.
The UK's actions demonstrate a continued focus on Russia's energy revenues, sanctions circumvention networks, and shadow fleet activities.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends Five Names on 1988 Sanctions List
body: On October 29, 2026, the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1988 (2011) enacted amendments to five entries on its 1988 List.
These amendments involve individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2816 (2026).
The changes were adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Removes Three Entries from ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: The Security Council Committee concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities removed three entries from its Sanctions List on October 24, 2026.
The delistings occurred after the Committee concluded its consideration of delisting requests submitted by the designating State.
This action aligns with paragraph 75 of resolution 2734 (2024).
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases

articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Law Firm and Shipping Agents Supporting Iran's Shadow Fleet
body: As part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury sanctioned Panama- and Greece-based law firm Karnakis and Karnakis on October 21, 2026.
The firm is accused of supporting illicit Iranian shipping activity for years, indirectly aiding Tehran's ability to fund its military, weapons, and nuclear programs.
Treasury also sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents directly aiding Iranian shadow fleet operations, emphasizing the expanded sanctions risk for those doing business with Iran.

articles.headline: FinCEN Proposes Rule Against Iran's A7 Shadow Banking Network
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) proposed a rule on October 1, 2026, to prohibit transmittals of funds regarding transactions involving the A7 Network's Sub-Agents.
This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targets the A7 Network, a shadow banking network with ties to Russia used by the Iranian regime to evade sanctions.

FinCEN also issued an Alert to help financial institutions detect and report suspicious activity related to the A7 Network, while OFAC sanctioned the network as a significant transnational criminal organization.

articles.headline: BIS Announces $2 Million Settlement with Lambda Research Corporation for Export Control Violations
body: On October 2, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced a $2 million administrative settlement with Massachusetts-based Lambda Research Corporation.

The settlement resolves 66 alleged violations of the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) involving exports of optical and illumination design software, automatic software updates, and transactions with parties on the Entity List and Unverified List.

Key takeaways from this enforcement action include that EAR99 software is not unrestricted, automatic software updates can constitute exports, and restricted-party screening must be ongoing throughout customer relationships.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
